section_summary: Pages 1–36 are a detailed list of papers summarizing documents about Japanese acquisition of petroleum, scrap metal, ores, cotton, rubber and other strategic materials, together with proposed export restrictions and widespread public and congressional protests. Pages 37–53 contain several of the indexed documents: correspondence with senators, constituent protests, and diplomatic reports from Colombia and Haiti. Pages 54–55 begin an Office of Production Management memorandum identifying Latin American sources of strategic-material “leakage” to Japan and recommending stronger purchasing and export-control measures.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Army Equipment and Supplies—Japan
subfiles.about: A detailed index describes correspondence and reports on Japanese acquisition of strategic commodities and United States policy toward those exports.
subfiles.summary: The list covers document numbers roughly 1247–1562 and records telegrams, despatches, memoranda, letters and congressional inquiries dated principally from January through August 1941. Major subjects include petroleum, scrap iron, tungsten, cobalt, lead, manganese, cotton, rubber, asbestos and other materials obtained from the United States, Latin America, the Philippines and European or Asian sources. It also documents export-control policy, proposed embargo legislation, diplomatic consultations and numerous public protests against assisting Japan.

subfiles.title: Department of State routing sheet for file 894.24/1253
subfiles.about: A departmental routing sheet identifies file 894.24/1253.
subfiles.summary: Nearly blank routing sheet for file 894.24/1253, covering correspondence on gasoline and petroleum exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Houston Committee resolution against petroleum shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: Robert F. Peden and Rolland Bradley, Houston Committee to Defend America by Aiding the Allies
subfiles.about: The Houston Committee asks Senator Connally to help stop gasoline and petroleum shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Houston Committee says about 100,000 barrels of gasoline monthly leave Texas ports, mainly for Japan, which could upgrade it for aviation; urges passing the Lend-Lease bill.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Connally on gasoline export controls
subfiles.about: The State Department explains the licensing controls applicable to gasoline capable of being upgraded for aviation use.
subfiles.summary: Reply to Senator Connally: regulations already require licenses for lower-grade gasoline raisable by tetraethyl lead; controls adjusted to defense needs; original letter returned.

subfiles.title: Senator Harrison’s inquiry concerning war-material exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Senator Harrison forwards G. B. Harper’s protest and requests an explanation of continuing war-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Harper says Americans believed sales of war materials to Japan had stopped and fears use against servicemen and Britain; Harrison asks Hull for a reply to send constituents.

subfiles.title: Secretary Hull’s reply to Senator Harrison on export controls
subfiles.about: Hull outlines the Export Control Act and the government’s licensing policy for strategic exports.
subfiles.summary: Hull encloses the July 2, 1940 Export Control Act and proclamations; controlled goods go to the Empire and hemisphere from surplus, scrap barred elsewhere, other exports sparingly licensed.

subfiles.title: Germans in Colombia advised to purchase hides for Japanese vessels
subfiles.about: The embassy reports that a Japanese trading agent asked a German resident of Riohacha to acquire hides and skins for shipment on Japanese vessels.
subfiles.summary: Yujiro Kunimatsu of Oriental Trading reportedly asked William Eikoff for cow hides and goat and sheep skins for Japanese ships soon to visit Colombian and Venezuelan ports.

subfiles.title: Sale of Haitian cotton to Japan
subfiles.from: Edward J. Sparks, American Legation, Port-au-Prince
subfiles.about: The legation reports a Japanese contract for 632 metric tons of Haitian cotton.
subfiles.summary: C. Itoh of Osaka, through broker Victor Mansour, contracted to buy 632 metric tons of Haitian cotton for April or May delivery at $9.00 and $8.50 per 50 kilograms, cancellable if shipment impossible.

subfiles.title: Charter of the motor ship Janko for a California–Japan fuel-oil cargo
subfiles.about: The writer reports Mitsubishi’s charter of the motor ship Janko and other prospective petroleum cargoes.
subfiles.summary: The 13,500-ton Janko was chartered for a March California-Japan fuel-oil cargo at $20 a ton; Mitsubishi chartered another tanker; a Russian solar-oil cargo confirmed.

subfiles.title: Inquiry concerning scrap-iron shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Representative Beckworth asks whether scrap iron is currently being exported from the United States to Japan and in what quantity.
subfiles.summary: Beckworth asks the Secretary to state how much scrap iron, if any, is being shipped to Japan.

subfiles.title: Senator Sheppard transmits Martin Thompson’s protest
subfiles.about: Senator Sheppard forwards a constituent’s complaint about iron shipments to Japan and asks for a reply.
subfiles.summary: Sheppard encloses Mrs. Martin Thompson's letter and asks for an answer to pass on.

subfiles.title: Martin Thompson’s protest against iron shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: A Houston constituent condemns continued iron exports to Japan and asks why they are permitted.
subfiles.summary: Thompson learned iron still leaves Houston for Japan, calls it unchristian and unwise, and says the US cannot claim friendship with China while arming its enemy.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Sheppard on iron and steel export controls
subfiles.about: The Department explains the statutory controls on scrap iron and other iron and steel exports.
subfiles.summary: Reply to Sheppard: Export Control Act enclosed; scrap barred outside the Empire and hemisphere, other iron and steel exports sparingly licensed; Thompson's letter returned.

subfiles.title: Strategic materials from Latin America being shipped to Japan
subfiles.about: The memorandum identifies strategic materials moving from Latin America to Japan and proposes measures to close important supply channels.
subfiles.summary: Memo on Latin American strategic materials reaching Japan, stressing Mexico, Bolivia and Brazil: Mexican zinc, mercury and copper, Japanese outbidding for Bolivian tungsten, Brazilian mica; recommends faster central purchasing with Britain.
